sections.title: Reading Comprehension · Passage B
sections.intro: Read “Storm Warnings” and answer questions 10–14. Vocabulary notes follow the poem.

lines.text: The glass¹ has been falling all the afternoon,
And knowing better than the instrument
What winds are walking overhead, what zone
Of gray unrest is moving across the land,
I leave the book upon a pillowed chair
And walk from window to closed window, watching
The stiff boughs strain against the blotted sky
And think again, as often when the air
Moves inward toward a silent core of waiting,
How with a single purpose time has traveled
Through currents of unguessed fatality
Into this polar realm, this present island.
Weather abroad and weather in the heart
Alike come on regardless of prediction.
Between foreseeing and averting change
Lies all the mastery of elements
Which clocks and weather-glasses cannot alter.
Time in the hand is not control of time,
Nor shattered fragments of an instrument
The breaking of a cordon² of events.
The wind will rise: we can only close the shutters.
I draw the curtains as the sky goes black
And set a match to candles sheathed in glass
Against the keyhole draught,³ the insistent whine
Of weather through the unsealed aperture.⁴
This is our sole defense against the season;
These are the things that we have learned to do
Who live in zones of much inquietude.⁵
¹ glass — barometer
² cordon — string
³ draught — draft
⁴ aperture — an opening
⁵ inquietude — a disturbance

questions.prompt: The figurative language used in lines 9 through 11 suggests the
questions.explanation: The waiting air and time moving toward “unguessed fatality” evoke an approaching event that cannot yet be known, like a challenge that life is about to bring.

questions.prompt: The purpose of the repetition of “weather” in line 13 is to imply
questions.explanation: “Weather abroad” describes the outer storm, while “weather in the heart” links it to the speaker’s inner feelings. The repetition makes the storm personal.

questions.prompt: The statement, “The wind will rise: we can only close the shutters” (line 21) most likely means we

choices.text: can overcome problems by denying them
cannot predict our emotions but we can learn to ignore them
can control events by understanding them
cannot prevent our distress but we can choose how to deal with it

questions.explanation: The wind is beyond the speaker’s control, but closing the shutters is a deliberate response. Similarly, people cannot stop every distressing event but can choose their response.

questions.prompt: Lines 27 and 28 convey a sense of
questions.explanation: The speaker describes sheltering from storms as what people in unsettled places have learned to do. That matter-of-fact recognition conveys acceptance.

questions.prompt: The poem suggests that the narrator views storms as
questions.explanation: The speaker says the same kind of unsettled weather returns and describes familiar protective acts—closing shutters, drawing curtains, lighting candles. Storms are a recurring part of life.
